---
title: "Exercise 5: Undo a change safely"
description: "Use git revert to undo a commit without rewriting history."
---

**Goal**: undo a commit that has already been pushed, the safe way.

## 1. Make a change you'll regret

1. Create a branch `alex/revert-practice` from an up-to-date `main`.
2. In `index.qmd`, change the heading `# Victorian Cancer Screening Statistical Report` to `# Victorian Cancer Screening Statistical Repot` (a typo).
3. Commit with the message `Update title` and push.

## 2. Revert it

Pretend this was merged and published. You can't delete the commit, because other people may already have it. Instead, add a **new** commit that does the opposite. In the **Terminal** tab of either IDE:

```bash
git log --oneline -3
git revert --no-edit HEAD
```

Git creates a commit with the message `Revert "Update title"`. Push it as usual.

## 3. Check

::: {.panel-tabset group="ide"}
## RStudio

Git pane → **History**. Both commits are there: the mistake and its revert. `index.qmd` is back to the original text.

## Positron

Source Control Graph shows both commits. `index.qmd` is back to the original text.

## Terminal

```bash
git log --oneline -3
git diff HEAD~2 HEAD -- index.qmd   # no output: the net change is nothing
```
:::

**Revert, don't rewrite.** Commands like `git reset --hard` and force-pushing delete history; on a shared branch they cause problems for everyone else. `git revert` is always safe.

To revert an older commit, use its ID from `git log --oneline`, e.g. `git revert 3f2a1bc`.
